title: Page Travel Guide

hero.headline: Page Travel Guide
hero.subheadline: Use Page as a compact high-desert base for Lake Powell, Glen Canyon, Horseshoe Bend, and permitted Navajo Nation slot-canyon experiences.

overview: Page was developed near Glen Canyon Dam and today functions primarily as a gateway to the Colorado River, Lake Powell, Glen Canyon National Recreation Area, and nearby Navajo Nation landscapes.

The key planning distinction is jurisdiction: Glen Canyon is managed by the National Park Service, while Antelope Canyon and several other slot canyons are on Navajo Nation land and require authorized access.

highlights.title: Lake Powell and Glen Canyon
highlights.description: Reservoir, canyon, and river landscapes dominate the region around Page.

highlights.title: Horseshoe Bend
highlights.description: The Colorado River makes a dramatic entrenched meander just outside the city.

highlights.title: Navajo Nation slot canyons
highlights.description: Antelope Canyon and other guided slot-canyon experiences are on Navajo Nation land, not city or NPS property.

highlights.title: Glen Canyon Dam
highlights.description: The dam and nearby overlooks explain why Page exists and how the modern reservoir landscape formed.

thingsToDo.title: Visit Horseshoe Bend
thingsToDo.description: Use the designated parking area and trail to the overlook. Go early or late for cooler conditions and better light.

thingsToDo.title: Tour Antelope Canyon with an authorized operator
thingsToDo.description: Upper and Lower Antelope Canyon are on Navajo Nation land and require authorized guided access. Book well ahead in peak periods.

thingsToDo.title: Explore Lake Powell
thingsToDo.description: Boat tours, paddling, and shoreline recreation reveal the flooded canyon landscape. Check current water levels and launch conditions.

thingsToDo.title: See Glen Canyon Dam and the Colorado River corridor
thingsToDo.description: The dam, bridge, and nearby viewpoints provide context for regional water management and canyon geography.

thingsToDo.title: Visit Glen Canyon National Recreation Area
thingsToDo.description: NPS-managed lands surround much of Page; check current access, fees, and closures before heading out.

thingsToDo.title: Consider other permitted slot-canyon experiences
thingsToDo.description: Page has multiple guided canyon options beyond Antelope Canyon. Verify operator authorization and physical difficulty before booking.

bestTimeToVisit.title: Spring and fall usually offer the best balance
bullets: Summer heat can be intense, especially on exposed trails and in parking areas.
Spring and fall are popular for boating and hiking, so reserve tours early.
Winter is quieter and cooler; some water-based operations may have reduced schedules.

travelTips: Carry more water than you think you need; shade is limited at many viewpoints.
Treat Antelope Canyon timing and access rules separately from NPS sites.
Check lake levels and ramp availability before boating.
Page is compact, but most major landscapes require driving or a guided tour.

faq.q: How many days should I spend in Page?
faq.a: Two to three days covers Horseshoe Bend, a slot-canyon tour, and time on or around Lake Powell.
It is near Page on Navajo Nation land, not a city attraction. Access is controlled through authorized guided tours.

faq.q: Is Lake Powell a national park?
faq.a: No. Much of the surrounding federal recreation area is Glen Canyon National Recreation Area, managed by the National Park Service.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Page is an incorporated northern Arizona city built as a service and gateway community near Glen Canyon Dam.

sections.heading: Geography & setting
paragraphs: The city sits on the Colorado Plateau near Glen Canyon, the Colorado River, Lake Powell, and Navajo Nation lands.

sections.heading: History & culture
paragraphs: Modern Page grew from the Glen Canyon Dam construction era, while the surrounding landscape has far older Indigenous history.

sections.heading: Outdoor highlights
paragraphs: Boating, paddling, canyon touring, photography, and desert hiking dominate visitor itineraries.

sections.heading: Getting around
paragraphs: A car or guided tour is essential for most major sights, and access rules differ sharply by land manager.
